analysis.one_liner: Raises government milk price supports and guarantees dairy farmers a higher price for their milk.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or vote in the 102nd Congress and died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the government-set price floor for milk by about 25%, from $10.10 to $12.63 per hundredweight, and required the Agriculture Department to keep raising it whenever milk prices fell below farm production costs [S3]. It would have given each dairy farm a guaranteed production quota, paying the full market price on the quota and only the low world-market price on milk produced beyond it [S3]. It also would have created an advisory board mostly made up of dairy producers to guide how milk surpluses are cut back, and set minimum milk-solids content for whole, lowfat, and skim milk [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Dairy farmers, particularly producers in high-output states, would gain a higher guaranteed price, an income floor tied to their cost of production indexed to inflation, and production quotas that lock in their historical sales volumes and are transferable when a farm changes hands [S3]. Government purchases of surplus butter, cheese, and nonfat dry milk would continue, and dairy cooperatives and exporters could bid to buy those surpluses [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Raises the milk price support rate from $10.10 to $12.63 per hundredweight, roughly a 25% increase in the government-guaranteed price [S3].

Requires the Secretary of Agriculture to raise the support price to the cost of producing milk, adjusted annually for inflation, whenever average milk prices run low for 120 consecutive days, giving producers an automatic income floor [S3].

Sets a production level for each dairy farm based on 1989-1991 sales volumes, transfers it to new owners who keep dairying, and pays full support on the quota portion, protecting established farms' market position [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers would pay more for milk and dairy products because the government floor raises the price all milk trades around. Taxpayers would bear the cost of the government buying and disposing of surplus butter, cheese, and nonfat dry milk when the high support price pushes production beyond demand, a cost the bill explicitly prices into the lower rate paid on surplus milk [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill acknowledges its own cost problem: surplus milk would be paid only the world market price minus disposal costs, because paying full support on everything would leave the government holding expensive surpluses — a pattern that had cost taxpayers heavily under prior milk support programs [S3].

Higher support prices translate into higher retail milk prices for households, a cost that falls hardest on low-income families, and the two of eighteen board seats set aside for consumers left producers and processors holding most of the say over supply policy [S3].

Production quotas based on 1989-1991 sales would freeze the structure of the industry around existing farms, making it harder for new entrants and for efficient producers to expand, and raising costs of milk for manufacturers of cheese, butter, and other products [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For dairy farmers this was a serious income-protection bill, and the two-tier design and surplus disposal rules showed awareness of the surplus-storage problem that plagued older price support programs. But the fundamental trade still runs from the many to the few: a 25% higher government floor means higher grocery prices for every milk-drinking household and continued taxpayer-funded purchases of surplus dairy products, all to lift incomes in one regionally concentrated industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Agriculture Committee, which took no further action on it before the 102nd Congress ended, so it died without a hearing or vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Robert Kasten introduced the bill on July 16, 1991, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry [S1] [S5].
No additional legislative action — no hearing, markup, committee report, or floor vote — was ever recorded on the bill for the remainder of the 102nd Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers and taxpayers are better off that it died: they avoided a roughly 25% higher milk price floor and the government purchases of surplus dairy products it would have required. Dairy farmers in states like Wisconsin lost the chance at the higher guaranteed price and production quotas it offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers and taxpayers, who paid no higher milk floor

for.name: Sen. Robert W. Kasten Jr.
for.role: U.S. Senator from Wisconsin; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise milk price supports and create production quotas for dairy farms.

against.name: Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or report was ever held.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan lineup ever formed before it died in committee.

industries.note: The bill's entire purpose is a roughly 25% higher government-guaranteed milk price plus cost-of-production indexing and individual production quotas. The gain comes from higher retail milk prices and taxpayer-funded purchases of surplus dairy products, so it runs against ordinary households' pocketbooks.

They could bid to acquire surplus cheese, butter, and nonfat dry milk held by the Commodity Credit Corporation, and cooperatives shared in the higher support prices. Consumers, meanwhile, faced the higher prices that generate the surplus.

Handlers would have had to pay the near-world-market price on surplus milk under federal marketing orders, and beverage processors would have had to meet new minimum milk-solids requirements — added costs. Five of eighteen seats on the new Industry Marketing Board would have gone to processors, giving them a say in supply policy.
